turns: List the observed operation nodes in this worker.

lines: Describe returned nodes and edges as observed graph structure.

State when a section is empty or omitted from the result.
Give me a live overview of all workers.
Show me the graph for this worker.
What about the graph for the other worker?
Resolve the follow-up using the earlier worker overview and retrieve the other worker's graph.
Keep graph evidence attached to the PID returned for that worker.
If the inventory does not identify one unambiguous other worker, ask for clarification instead of reusing the selected worker's graph.

turns: Show recent events from this worker and summarize their timestamps, services, and probes.

lines: Summarize only returned event fields and preserve trace IDs when relevant.
Do not treat event timestamps as event durations or infer missing events.
Find a trace ID in this worker's recent events, then inspect that
trace's critical path and summarize the returned stage durations.
Use a trace ID actually returned by the event query and keep it consistent.

Select a trace whose observed event type matches the request; for request critical paths prefer request start/entry and exit/end boundaries, and for worker lifecycle questions use spawn/start/ready/exit events.
Describe every returned trace stage's duration_ms exactly as returned, and state when a stage has no returned duration.
Do not calculate stage durations by subtracting event timestamps or invent stages absent from get_worker_trace.
Do not claim a component caused latency without supporting trace evidence.
Find a trace ID in this worker's recent events and stitch that exact
trace across live worker processes. Summarize which PIDs contributed.
Use the exact trace ID obtained from events and list only PIDs found in the stitched result.
Report a partial or empty result as such; do not imply every live process participated.
Keep returned per-worker inter-event durations separate; do not calculate cross-process latency from timestamps.

turns: Show saved causal-rule history for this selected worker and summarize any recorded matches.

lines: Report only history records returned for the selected worker instance.
Distinguish saved matches from a fresh live rule evaluation.
Treat an empty history result as no saved records returned, not proof no rule ever matched.

turns: Show the current status of this worker and tell me whether it has active requests.

lines: Answer from the selected process instance's uploaded status heartbeat and graph snapshot.
Report heartbeat freshness, uptime, and active-request count when present; include the active probes and rules when the user asks which are loaded.
If the heartbeat is missing or stale, say that current health/activity cannot be established instead of describing the process as currently healthy.
Identify missing details instead of guessing.
For this selected worker, summarize its status, observed graph
structure, and currently matched causal-rule patterns. Explain
plausible operational risks suggested by that evidence, while
separating detected patterns from hypotheses and not claiming a
root cause.
Report status, graph nodes and edges, and rule matches only for the selected worker.
Distinguish registered rules, matched patterns, and registered rules with no match in the returned evaluation.
Treat a causal-rule match and graph structure as patterns or relationships, not proof of root cause or impact.
Describe risks as plausible implications supported by observations, and state when evidence cannot establish system impact or causation.
Cite findings with valid evidence IDs and avoid unsupported remediation advice.
For db_query_hotspot, report the exact query-level call counts, percentages, and averages from the rule evidence; do not swap values between queries or infer user counts.
Do not turn a detected hotspot into a claim that database load caused request latency.
Do not add unresolved questions or remediation steps about authentication, caching, or N+1 behavior unless the user asks and evidence supports the specific claim.
Give me an overview of all live OriginTracer workers.
For each worker, summarize status, graph structure, and matched causal-rule patterns.
Explain plausible operational risks only where the evidence supports them,
and distinguish patterns from confirmed causes.
Use the dedicated all-worker overview and report only identities present in its inventory result.
Summarize status, graph node/edge counts or returned graph details, and matched rule patterns per worker.
Identify per-worker query errors and graph truncation when present.
Count only workers with fresh heartbeats as currently reporting; identify stale snapshots separately and do not call them live workers.
Treat matched rules and graph topology as patterns, not proof of cause or system impact.
Describe plausible risks only as qualified implications supported by the returned observations.
Identify workers by returned PID and keep each worker’s status, probe set, graph counts, and rule matches attached to that PID; never transfer a value from one worker to another.
Do not claim workers have similar or identical patterns unless the returned values support that comparison.
A node named NPlusOneView does not prove an N+1 query pattern. Distinguish a matched db_query_hotspot rule from a matched n_plus_one_queries rule.
Report exact average durations as per-call averages. Do not multiply duration by call_count or infer per-user or per-request impact.
Do not recommend caching, code changes, synthetic testing, or other remediation unless requested and supported by evidence.
Give me an operational overview of the current runtime, including
status, graphs, causal patterns, and plausible risks.
When a worker is already selected and the requested overview scope is ambiguous, ask whether to inspect all workers or only the selected worker.
After the supplied answer selects all, use the all-worker overview tool and report per-worker scope accurately.
Do not treat detected rule patterns as confirmed causes.
Find the busiest operation in this worker, inspect recent events,
and explain what the evidence shows about its activity.
Use both hotspot and event evidence to answer.
Distinguish observed activity from an explanation of why it is happening.
For this Django worker, compare slow database queries with asyncio
event-loop starvation as possible explanations for high request latency.
Inspect database query latency and events as well as event-loop evidence.
Gather evidence for and against each explanation, and say what remains unclear.
Use duration-ranked database nodes and django.db.query events to
assess the database explanation, and inspect live causal-rule matches.
If db_query_hotspot is present, report it as a call-count pattern with
its evidence citation, not proof of slow queries or root cause.
Separate event-loop activity from evidence of starvation.
Do not treat absence from HOTSPOT TOP as evidence that database work
is absent or fast. Do not claim a root cause unless the evidence
supports it; state what remains unclear and what evidence is missing.
Check this Django worker for configured N+1 query and database query
hotspot patterns. Explain what any matching rules detect, and what
they do not prove.
Use live rule results for n_plus_one_queries and db_query_hotspot
when configured. Explain their match evidence accurately: an N+1
match relates query count to view count; a database hotspot reflects
a high share of database calls. Do not treat either match or confidence
as proof that it caused latency. If a rule is absent, distinguish no
match from a rule not being configured. Cite valid evidence IDs.
Check this worker for configured asyncio event-loop starvation and
post-deployment synchronous-call patterns. Explain the rule evidence
and remaining uncertainty.
Inspect live asyncio and deployment-related rule matches when
configured. A match is a pattern detected over the current aggregate
graph, not proof of request-level causality. Do not infer loop health
from ordinary tick activity or infer that no rule is configured from
an empty match list. Cite valid evidence IDs and state limitations.
Check this worker for configured LangGraph runaway-loop and LLM/tool
latency-hotspot rules. Explain what any match means and what remains
unproven.
Inspect registered LangGraph rule names and live matches. Explain that
loop_runaway compares LLM calls with graph invocations, while
agent_latency_hotspot identifies a node's share of aggregate leaf-work
time. Do not claim either proves a root cause for one request. Cite
valid evidence IDs and describe missing probe or workload evidence.
Find the busiest operation in this worker and summarize the evidence.
Check whether the recent events add evidence about that same operation.
Use the second request as a follow-up to the first investigation.
Keep the answer focused on the same selected worker and relate new
observations to prior evidence.
Treat this as a factual check for whether recent events show the
previously identified busiest operation. Do not invent causal
hypotheses or use sampled events to claim that an operation never
occurs. The report should not expand into latency diagnoses for
other routes. Event probe filters are exact instrumentation probe
names, not graph node IDs; inspect service events with no probe
filter for matching operation names. Event timestamps do not establish
durations; only report durations supplied as duration measurements.
Keep the final report scoped to the second request: include the earlier hotspot evidence only as needed to assess the new events, and do not replay unrelated status or graph sections.

turns: How many workers are currently being monitored?
Are those workers healthy, and should I be worried?
Which worker is showing both asyncio starvation and database hotspots?

lines: Treat the third request as a factual follow-up about the patterns discussed in the immediately preceding worker-health answer.
Identify the PID whose own overview data shows both asyncio_event_loop_starvation and db_query_hotspot, citing that overview evidence.
Answer the latest question directly. Do not repeat the original worker count or replay the full health assessment.
Do not carry hypotheses from the health assessment into this factual query or describe either rule match as a confirmed cause.
Compare database latency and asyncio event-loop starvation as
possible explanations for this worker's high request latency.
Inspect diagnostics and summarize evidence for each.
For those two explanations, what does the evidence support or
weaken, and what remains unclear?
Treat the second turn as a follow-up to the two hypotheses in the
first investigation. Reuse its diagnostic evidence rather than
treating the follow-up as unrelated.
Without request-correlated component durations, keep both causal
hypothesis reviews inconclusive. Report the database hotspot and
asyncio measurements as patterns or measurements, not causes, and
state that their relationship to request latency remains unknown.
Do not repeat either hypothesis as a factual finding or recommend
optional next investigations.
Keep the final report scoped to the second request, reusing the prior diagnostic evidence without repeating unrelated report sections.
Show this worker's graph and summarize the observed nodes and
edges.
What is this worker's current status and uptime?
Treat the status question as a new investigation even though it
arrives on the same checkpointed thread. Answer from status evidence
and do not carry forward the unrelated graph inventory.
The final report should contain the current status answer only; do not replay the previous graph report or other unrelated observations.
Compare the most frequently called operations with the slowest
database queries on this worker. Explain what each ranking measures
and whether either one establishes a cause of request latency.
Use both tool results and explicitly explain the metric each ranks:
get_worker_hotspots ranks node call counts; get_worker_database_hotspots
ranks database nodes by average duration. Treat total_duration_ms as
an aggregate across calls, not the ranking key or a single request's
latency. Do not equate frequent calls with slow queries, claim either
ranking proves request-level impact, or call a query absolutely slow
without a baseline. State directly whether these results establish
request impact. For this answered metric comparison, leave the
unresolved-question and next-step lists empty; do not invent causal
hypotheses or optional follow-up work. If a
ranking is empty or unavailable, report that limit without inferring
no activity.
Show the busiest operation and use the worker graph to identify
what calls it. Summarize the observed relationship without guessing
why the operation is frequent.
Use the hotspot result to identify high call volume and either the
edge list or combined graph result to describe caller-to-callee
relationships when present. Treat call counts and graph structure
as observations, not proof of a loop, bug, or performance cause.
State when the graph does not identify a caller. Use complete
operation names present in the evidence; do not call a name truncated
or recommend retrieving it when the full name is supplied.
Check what changed in this worker's graph since the deployment
marker. Summarize added or removed nodes and edges, and say what
those structural changes can and cannot tell us.
Report the returned changes or explain if there is no usable marker
or comparison baseline. Structural graph differences show changed
observations; they do not alone establish why a change occurred or
whether it caused latency. Cite recorded evidence.

lines: Explain that the N+1 rule compares a database query call count with its calling view and detects a ratio of at least five to one.
Explain that the database hotspot rule detects a query pattern making up more than 30% of observed database calls.
Clearly distinguish the two patterns and avoid claiming either match proves a root cause.
Cite the official Django causal rules documentation page.
